```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
options(width = 72)
```

The columns of an fMRI array are voxels, or surface vertices, or parcels, or
latent components. A frame's *feature space* says which. It gives every
column a stable ID, knows where each one is, and can turn a row of values back
into a brain image or surface map. This vignette introduces each kind of
space, shows how selections restrict a space, explains when two spaces count
as the same, and moves a frame from one space to another. It assumes the
basics from `vignette("fmridataset")`.

```{r}
library(fmridataset)
library(Matrix)
```

## A masked volume

`volume_space()` describes voxels on a 3-D grid: the grid dimensions, the
voxel-to-world affine, and the *support*, the voxels inside the mask. Each
voxel in the support gets an ID from its position on the grid, so the IDs stay
the same however the voxels are later selected or reordered.

```{r volume}
grid <- c(4L, 4L, 2L)
mask <- array(FALSE, grid)
mask[2:3, 2:3, ] <- TRUE

brain <- volume_space(dim = grid, support = mask, template = "toy")
brain
feature_ids(brain)
head(feature_data(brain), 3)
```

The feature table gives each voxel its linear index and grid coordinates, so
`select_features()` can choose voxels by position. The rest of the vignette
uses a frame of six volumes over this space.

```{r frame}
set.seed(2)
bold <- matrix(
  round(rnorm(6 * n_features(brain)), 2),
  nrow = 6, ncol = n_features(brain)
)
frame <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = bold),
  observations = data.frame(
    .obs_id = sprintf("vol-%02d", 1:6),
    run_id = "run-1",
    TR = 2
  ),
  space = brain
)
```

## Surfaces and plain indices

`surface_space()` describes the vertices of a cortical mesh, each labelled
with its hemisphere. Vertices on the medial wall, which carry no cortical
signal, can be left out of the support; they keep their IDs but are not
columns of the frame.

```{r surface}
left <- surface_space(
  vertex_ids = sprintf("L%d", 1:5),
  hemisphere = "left",
  medial_wall = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE),
  template = "toy-mesh"
)
left
feature_ids(left)
```

The mesh geometry is optional. `surface_space_from_neurosurf()` reads it,
with the vertex adjacency, from a `neurosurf` surface.

When the columns have no spatial layout at all, such as summary values for a
list of regions, `index_space()` simply names them.

```{r index}
regions <- index_space(3, ids = c("amygdala", "hippocampus", "insula"))
regions
```

## Selections restrict the space

A view's feature space is the original space restricted to the selected
features, in the selected order. The restricted space still knows its grid,
its affine, and where its voxels are.

```{r restrict}
pair <- frame[, c("voxel-11", "voxel-6")]
space(pair)
same_space(space(pair), restrict_space(brain, c(4L, 1L)))
```

Selecting nothing is legal and gives a space with no features, which is what
a `select_features()` that matches nothing returns.

```{r restrict-empty}
n_features(restrict_space(brain, integer()))
```

Any row of a frame can be turned back into an image. For a volume that is a
`neuroim2` `NeuroVol` with `NA` outside the support; from a view, the voxels
that were not selected are `NA` as well.

```{r spatial-map}
image <- spatial_map(frame, "vol-01")
dim(image)
sum(!is.na(image))
sum(!is.na(spatial_map(pair, "vol-01")))
```

## Same space, not merely same size

`same_space()` returns `TRUE` only when two spaces agree on their type, their
digest, and their ordered feature IDs. A space built again from the same grid,
affine, support, and template is the same space.

```{r same-space}
again <- volume_space(dim = grid, support = mask, template = "toy")
same_space(brain, again)
```

Change the affine and the voxels keep their IDs but sit somewhere else in the
world, so the spaces differ. The result says which part differs.

```{r different-space}
rescaled <- volume_space(
  dim = grid, affine = diag(c(2, 2, 2, 1)), support = mask, template = "toy"
)
same_space(brain, rescaled)
```

`same_space()` answers only whether two spaces are identical. Whether data can
move from one space to another is a separate question, answered by feature
maps, below. `assert_same_space()` turns a difference into an error; it is
what `bind_observations()` and `map_features()` check first.

```{r assert-space, error = TRUE}
assert_same_space(brain, rescaled)
```

## Parcels over a volume

A `parcel_space()` groups the features of a parent space into parcels through
a membership matrix with one row per parent feature and one column per
parcel. Here the two slices of the masked volume become two parcels.

```{r parcel}
slice <- feature_data(brain)$k
membership <- sparseMatrix(
  i = seq_len(n_features(brain)), j = slice, x = 1,
  dims = c(n_features(brain), 2L)
)
slabs <- parcel_space(
  parent = brain,
  parcel_ids = c("lower", "upper"),
  membership = membership,
  atlas = "slab",
  data = data.frame(
    id = c("lower", "upper"),
    label = c("Lower slab", "Upper slab")
  )
)
slabs
feature_ids(slabs)
```

The atlas name is part of every parcel ID, so parcels from different atlases
can never be confused. By default a parcel's value is the mean of its
members; ask for sums with `aggregation = "sum"`.
`parcel_space_from_atlas()` builds the same object from a `neuroatlas` atlas.

## Moving a frame between spaces

A parcel space knows how to compute its values from its parent, so
`map_features()` needs only the target. The result is a frame in the parcel
space whose assay is computed lazily, when it is read.

```{r map-parcel}
by_parcel <- map_features(frame, target = slabs)
by_parcel
collect_assay(by_parcel)
```

Those are the means of each slice, as a direct computation confirms.

```{r map-parcel-check}
direct <- cbind(
  rowMeans(bold[, slice == 1]),
  rowMeans(bold[, slice == 2])
)
all.equal(unname(collect_assay(by_parcel)), direct)
```

The new frame records the mapping in its provenance, and its rows turn back
into images by spreading each parcel's value over its voxels.

```{r map-parcel-provenance}
provenance(by_parcel)
range(spatial_map(by_parcel, "vol-01"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

Any other linear transformation is an explicit `feature_map()`: a
target-by-source matrix together with both spaces. Here each target feature
is the mean of two voxels.

```{r feature-map}
pairs <- index_space(2L, ids = c("pair-a", "pair-b"))
operator <- sparseMatrix(
  i = c(1, 1, 2, 2), j = c(1, 2, 3, 4), x = 0.5,
  dims = c(2L, n_features(brain))
)
pair_means <- feature_map(
  from = brain, to = pairs, operator = operator, map_type = "pair_mean"
)
pair_means
collect_assay(map_features(frame, map = pair_means))[1:2, ]
```

A map declared from a different space is refused, even though its matrix has
the right shape.

```{r feature-map-mismatch, error = TRUE}
wrong <- feature_map(from = rescaled, to = pairs, operator = operator)
map_features(frame, map = wrong)
```

## Latent components

A `basis_space()` describes components over a parent space, such as the
result of a PCA. It holds a *decoder*, which turns component scores into
parent values (one column of loadings per component), and an *encoder*, which
projects parent values onto the components. PCA loadings are a decoder; when
you have only a decoder, `basis_space_from_decoder()` derives the matching
least-squares encoder and checks it.

```{r basis}
loadings <- unname(prcomp(bold)$rotation[, 1:3])
components <- basis_space_from_decoder(
  parent = brain,
  component_ids = c("pc1", "pc2", "pc3"),
  decoder = loadings,
  basis_type = "pca"
)
components
```

With an encoder, `map_features()` projects a frame onto the components, and
`spatial_map()` rebuilds a volume from a row of scores.

```{r basis-map}
scores <- map_features(frame, target = components)
round(collect_assay(scores)[1:2, ], 3)
range(spatial_map(scores, "vol-01"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

`map_features()` projects the values as they are stored. `prcomp()` centres
each voxel first, so its `$x` differs from these scores by the projected
voxel means; centre the values before building the frame if you need
`prcomp()`'s scores exactly.

```{r basis-check}
all.equal(unname(collect_assay(scores)), bold %*% loadings)
```

Some decompositions cannot be inverted. An overcomplete dictionary has more
components than voxels, so no encoder can recover scores from voxel values.

```{r basis-overcomplete, error = TRUE}
dictionary <- matrix(rnorm(n_features(brain) * 10), n_features(brain), 10)
basis_space_from_decoder(
  parent = brain,
  component_ids = sprintf("atom-%02d", 1:10),
  decoder = dictionary
)
```

Ask for `encoder = "none"` and you get a *synthesis-only* basis: it can turn
scores into voxel values, but a frame cannot be mapped onto it. Frames of
scores, from the method that fitted the dictionary, are built directly in
that space.

```{r basis-synthesis-only}
atoms <- basis_space_from_decoder(
  parent = brain,
  component_ids = sprintf("atom-%02d", 1:10),
  decoder = dictionary,
  encoder = "none"
)
atoms

score_frame <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(scores = matrix(round(rnorm(6 * 10), 2), 6, 10)),
  observations = observations(frame),
  space = atoms
)
range(spatial_map(score_frame, "vol-01"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r basis-synthesis-error, error = TRUE}
map_features(frame, target = atoms)
```

## Combining spaces

A `composite_space()` joins several spaces into one feature axis, as CIFTI
grayordinates join two cortical surfaces and subcortical voxels. Feature IDs
are prefixed with the part name, and each part remains responsible for its own
features.

```{r composite}
right <- surface_space(
  vertex_ids = sprintf("R%d", 1:4),
  hemisphere = "right",
  template = "toy-mesh"
)
grayordinates <- composite_space(
  list(lh = left, rh = right, subcortex = brain),
  composite_type = "grayordinates"
)
grayordinates
feature_ids(grayordinates)[c(1, 5, 9)]
```

A frame over a composite space is selected and turned back into maps like any
other. Selecting the features of one part gives a composite that holds only
that part, and a map has one entry per part.

```{r composite-frame}
cifti <- fmri_frame(
  assays = list(bold = matrix(round(rnorm(6 * 16), 2), 6, 16)),
  observations = observations(frame),
  space = grayordinates
)
cortex <- select_features(cifti, .part %in% c("lh", "rh"))
space(cortex)
spatial_map(cifti, "vol-01")
```

## Where the package stops

`fmridataset` owns spatial identity, restriction, maps between spaces, and
applying those maps lazily. It does not register or resample images, fit
decompositions, choose atlases, or run models. `neuroatlas` supplies parcellations, `fmrilatent` supplies
fitted bases through `basis_space_from_fmrilatent()`, and `neurosurf` supplies
surface geometry through `surface_space_from_neurosurf()`. Each hands the
package a space; the package hands back frames whose columns still mean what
they meant.

To save frames in any of these spaces and reload them, see
`vignette("persistence-and-import")`.
